chapters.relation: The volume's introduction, 'Learning from the Insiders.' It introduces Orange Is the New Black (Piper Kerman's book and the Netflix series about Piper's time in Litchfield) and previews each contributor's topic: other minds, manipulation, the Prisoner's Dilemma, religion, existentialism, race, Crazy Eyes as Don Quixote, prisoners' moral obligations, Nietzsche on a trans woman, Aristotle on friendship, Bentham's panopticon, and Foucault on punishment. It frames the show as ripe for philosophy on punishment, moral obligation, existential themes, and race, gender, identity, and sexuality without itself applying any single theory.

chapters.file: ch10 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
ch11 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Hoyt argues the show's core lesson is dropping the little lies we tell ourselves: Bennett calls his crush on Daya 'love' to excuse framing Mendez, Pornstache is a man performing a blustering guard (Sartrean bad faith), and Larry and Polly's 'love just happened' dodges responsibility for betrayal. Piper's arc (the Colt 45 scene in '40 Oz. of Furlough') shows the payoff of authenticity, while Healy's Safe Place is a fantasy that cannot will a change of worldview. Using Wittgenstein's aspect-seeing from Philosophical Investigations, he shows how characters and viewers miss ethically significant meanings, like Taystee's shower 'compliment' as intimidation and Piper's convenient blindness to Soso's humanity when selling her for a blanket.

chapters.file: ch12 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Robison-Greene asks whether there are principled standards for 'shipping' TV couples and applies Platonic-Aristotelian flourishing criteria (long-term safety, emotional needs, trust, and mutual growth toward virtue) to Piper's options: Alex fails on safety and trust (selling Piper out, the perjury advice), Larry fails on empathy and growth, so by real-life standards we should ship none of them. She concludes shipping is mostly aesthetic, then proposes minimal moral rules for our attitudes toward fictional relationships: never ship Pornstache, respect consent, and never let race, gender, or orientation decide.

chapters.file: ch13 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
ch14 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: DiEdoardo, a trans criminal-defense lawyer, reads Sophia Burset through Nietzsche: her 'why of life' (bringing her body into line with her gender identity) lets her endure the 'how' of misgendering by Figueroa, Red, and her wife Crystal, plus a sentencing disparity she compares to Piper's lighter drug deal. Burset's rational appeals ('Lesbian Request Denied,' her WAC run) fail, confirming Nietzsche's disdain for dialectics, but in 'A Whole Other Hole' she stops asking and acts, teaching the inmates vulval anatomy until Taystee's 'she's right' marks her acceptance. She is the 'creator' who breaks the tables of values, migrating from freak to woman with unique knowledge.

chapters.file: ch15 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Carveth examines African-American portrayal on the show through Piper, Taystee, and Sophia: Piper's whiteness wins Healy's favoritism and makes her complicit in keeping the inmates powerless ('we understand each other, don't we?'), while Taystee's parole violation shows Litchfield as the only place she fits. Using Lippmann's account of media stereotypes, he credits the show with multidimensional characters of color but faults it for a 'white voice': Black women's incarceration is framed as bad choices and culture of poverty, and only Piper's SHU suffering is shown while Black and Latina women cycle through it. The series critiques the prison system yet stops short of showing the structural forces that leave its inmates no options.

chapters.file: ch16 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
ch17 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Ketcham greets Piper Kerman at the prison door with Bentham's ghost: the state's utility calculation of her drug money laundering, the rat's discounted sentence, and the design of the panopticon, whose one-way inspection tower was meant to make surveillance cheap, obedience automatic, and prisoners productive and even saved. He contrasts that reform vision with the reality reconstructed from the book, where punishment falls on everyone, including families paying commissary prices and denied visits, and Danbury's 'vocational training' amounts to changing light bulbs. Bentham's own principle that 'punishment is an evil' is turned against a system that warehouses rather than rehabilitates.

chapters.file: ch18 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Neal reads Litchfield through Sartre's No Exit: Alex, the ex who both agonizes and galvanizes Piper, makes the other inmates, not the walls, the hell of prison, just as Piper shouts 'I love you and I fucking hate you.' The 'Scared Straight' episode ('Bora Bora Bora') drives the deeper point when Piper tells Dina that the real punishment is coming face to face with who you are: 'I'm scared that I'm not myself in here and I'm scared that I am.' Stripped of distractions, Piper undergoes an existential crisis that forces the self-awareness authenticity requires, though prison's limits keep a fully authentic life out of reach.

chapters.file: ch19 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
ch20 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Stephenson and Waller start from disliking bland, marketable Piper and use Foucault's Discipline and Punish to argue that Litchfield is a microcosm of State power: arbitrary unwritten rules, counts, strip searches, and constant surveillance train prisoners into docile, compliant participants in capitalism, with specialist wardens, psychologists, and lawyers molding the abnormal into the normal. Prisoners specialize too (Red's kitchen, Nicky's ear, Vee's drugs) to survive, and specialization hides the surveillance. The show itself embodies the mechanism, making viewers aware they too live under the Panopticon, though deviants like Crazy Eyes and her standing pee keep open the possibility of refusing State values.

chapters.file: ch21 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Cherry uses Vee's season-two grooming of Taystee, Poussey, Nicky, Cindy, and Crazy Eyes to test philosophers' accounts of manipulation (covert influence, non-rational persuasion, targeting weaknesses, misleading truthfully). She shows Vee's skill is not virtue, since manipulation threatens autonomy by imposing a will the victim would not endorse (Kantian personhood denied) and employs dishonesty, predatoriness, disrespect, and laziness, with Machiavellian ends. The defense she prescribes is Socratic: reject purely emotional persuasion like the sophists' flattery, and live the examined life by checking premises and motives before being played.

chapters.file: ch22 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
ch23 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Robison-Greene argues Rawlsian ideal theory breaks down at Litchfield: Soso's hunger strike gets only cosmetic concessions from Caputo, Sophia's WAC human-rights platform loses to Taystee's realism, and Piper learns the council 'is basically bullshit,' showing how idealization made by the powerful ignores the lived facts of Mendoza's abusive marriage, Jimmy's 'compassionate' death sentence, and Sophia's denied hormones. Against taking a 'moral holiday' in prison, she proposes care ethics, with role-based duties sensitive to actual circumstances, as the morality that fits life inside, and suggests non-ideal theory may fit the outside world too.

chapters.file: ch24 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Walker contrasts Pennsatucky's Christian fundamentalism with Piper's secular humanism (Kurtz's six features) in their 'Fool Me Once' confrontation. With no God, Sartre's existence precedes essence makes Piper condemned to create her own meaning: owning her crime to her mother and confessing the Pennsatucky prank, while Red and Vee play Sartre's cafe waiter, reducing themselves to chef and dealer, and Pennsatucky's 'defender of the unborn' persona is de Beauvoir's sub-man sheltering behind ready-made values. Marx's opium-of-the-people analogy explains why comforting, unverifiable belief can block the authentic, responsible pursuit of a meaningful life.

chapters.file: ch25 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
ch26 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Archibald casts Crazy Eyes as the show's Don Quixote, read through Descartes's Meditations: like Descartes ridding himself of conditioned false beliefs, Suzanne slaps her head to 'reset' and question everything, and like Quixote she blames an inner evil enchanter when her noble illusions collapse. Her rationalist imagination (chivalry, poetry, Piper as her Dulcinea) produces false beliefs that hurt, above all her devoted service to the manipulative Vee, yet the same faculty creates the beauty, coping, and nobility that make an ugly prison survivable, so truth may not be all that matters.

chapters.file: ch27 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Felder stages Sartre against Merleau-Ponty on the mind-body problem and other minds, opening with the shower scene where Taystee's 'you got them TV titties' makes Piper an object under a gaze, as Pornstache's look converts being caught into shame. But Piper pulling her towel back to appraise her own breasts 'sees-with' Taystee, and the audience's access to Piper's feelings shows perception is shared, not solipsistic. Merleau-Ponty's incarnated subjectivity, the flesh of the opening credits' real inmates' eyes, and actors' embodied performances dissolve the problem of other minds that Sartre's alienated subject-object model leaves open.

chapters.file: ch28 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
ch29 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Duffy applies Susan Wolf's formula (subjective attraction meeting objective attractiveness) to Red's cooking, Poussey's friendship, and Taystee's library work, arguing these women meet the conditions yet still cannot live meaningful lives because Litchfield hands out 'chickens': WAC, the mock job fair, and the yard chicken are illusions of meaning designed to keep inmates quiet, as Healy admits with his bath-before-dinner analogy. Only projects that change the prison's conditions themselves, Piper's newsletter sting and Soso's hunger strike, are genuinely meaningful, and the yogic dharma of non-attachment (Yoga Jones's mandala advice) is a survival tool, not a substitute. She closes that guards too can find meaning, and have an obligation, in rehabilitating rather than punishing.

chapters.file: ch30 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Elsby and Luzecky use Nicomachean Ethics VIII to sort Litchfield's bonds: Red's kitchen empire runs on friendships of utility that dissolve when her pipeline closes, race pre-assigns everyone's default friends, and Vee, who sleeps with RJ before having him killed, is incapable of friendship in any sense. The chapter locates genuine Aristotelian friendship only in Red's concern that Nicky stay off heroin (wishing her good for her own sake) and reads Red's sparing of Vee, held by a plastic bag, as respect without care, the recognition of a kindred quality that distinguishes Red from her evil counterpart.

chapters.file: ch31 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: Greene reconstructs the Prisoner's Dilemma with Pennsatucky and Vee in separate interrogation rooms, then maps a variant onto 'Thirsty Bird': whatever Alex does, Piper is better off testifying against Kubra, yet mutual silence was the group-rational outcome the two pact on the van ride. Alex defects anyway, leaving Piper with perjury and no leniency, and Greene argues Piper should have done the 'rational' thing, since Balik's revenge is only a threat while extra time in Litchfield is a certain harm and Alex has always been willing to screw her. The episode shows why honor among the self-interested fails without trust.

chapters.file: ch32 - Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy.md
chapters.relation: The editors' appendix, 'Sugar and Spice and Some Things Not So Nice!,' argues that part of the show's success is our cultural obsession with women-in-prison stories, from the film Caged to tabloid celebrity mugshots. It then catalogues famous imprisoned women from history and today: Marie Antoinette and Eleanor of Aquitaine under house arrest, Elizabeth Bathory and Joan of Arc in castle towers, the Salem witches, Patty Hearst, Billie Holiday and Martha Stewart at Alderson, Pussy Riot in Russian penal colonies, Aileen Wuornos, and the Tower of London's Anne Boleyn and Anne Askew. The survey supplies the real history behind the women-in-prison genre that Litchfield reworks, with no single philosopher or theory applied.

holes.name: Media Stereotypes (Lippmann's 'pictures in our heads')
holes.what: Walter Lippmann's account of stereotypes as overgeneralized mental representations of social groups that media reinforce when direct contact with the group is lacking.
holes.why: Carveth's critique of how Orange Is the New Black both advances and reproduces stereotypes of Black women on television is built directly on Lippmann's Public Opinion and subsequent content-analysis research.

holes.name: White Privilege
holes.what: The unearned structural advantages white people receive in institutions and everyday interactions, typically invisible to those who hold them.
holes.why: The chapter's central argument is that Piper's whiteness buys Healy's favoritism, softer punishment, and narrative centrality while Black and Latina inmates' suffering goes unshown.

holes.name: Manipulation (covert, non-rational influence)
holes.what: Influencing someone through covert or non-rational means (emotion, deception, exploited weaknesses) so they choose what they would not rationally endorse.
holes.why: Cherry's entire chapter defines and morally evaluates Vee's manipulation of the Litchfield inmates using McGinn, Barnhill, Noggle, and Stanley, and the taxonomy has no slug for manipulation itself.

holes.name: Ideal vs Non-Ideal Theory
holes.what: The methodological debate over whether justice should be theorized for perfectly compliant conditions or built from actual unjust conditions, with critics arguing ideal theory conceals the perspective of the powerful.
holes.why: The chapter's core claim is that Rawls-style ideal theory is irrelevant in Litchfield and morality must start from the prisoners' real, non-ideal conditions.

holes.name: The Prisoner's Dilemma
holes.what: A game-theory thought experiment in which each party's self-interested dominant strategy leaves both worse off than if they had cooperated.
holes.why: Greene's chapter is an extended exposition of the Prisoner's Dilemma and applies a variant to Piper and Alex's testimony decisions at Kubra's trial.
